content.title: NC State graduate launches on Artemis II mission, set to become first woman to travel around the moon
content.text: CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (WNCN) — A North Carolina State University alumna is making history as part of the first crewed mission to travel to the moon in more than half a century. Christina Koch and three fellow astronauts launched Wednesday from the Kennedy Space Center aboard NASA’s Artemis II — a groundbreaking mission that will carry humans around the moon for the first time since the Apollo era. The four-person crew — three Americans and one Canadian — is expected to spend about 10 days traveling around the moon without landing before returning to Earth. Koch, who earned her bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and physics from N.C. State University in 2001, previously set the record for the longest single spaceflight by a woman at 328 days. “To be the person that got to actually fulfill those missions out there was just a dream come true,” Koch said during an address at N.C. State University in 2023. This photo provided by NASA shows NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Artemis II commander, from left, Victor Glover, Artemis II ...This photo provided by NASA shows NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Artemis II commander, from left, Victor Glover, Artemis II pilot, Christina Koch, Artemis II mission specialist, and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen, Artemis II mission specialist, right, in a group photograph as they visit NASA’s Artemis II SLS (Space Launch System) rocket and Orion spacecraft, Monday, March 30, 2026, at Launch Complex 39B of NASA’s Kennedy Space Center, in Cape Canaveral, Fla. (Bill Ingalls/NASA via AP)This photo provided by NASA shows NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Artemis II commander, from left, Victor Glover, Artemis II pilot, Christina Koch, Artemis II mission specialist, and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen, Artemis II mission specialist, right, in a group photograph as they visit NASA’s Artemis II SLS (Space Launch System) rocket and Orion spacecraft, Monday, March 30, 2026, at Launch Complex 39B of NASA’s Kennedy Space Center, in Cape Canaveral, Fla. (Bill Ingalls/NASA via AP) Before attending college in Raleigh, the Onslow County native graduated from the North Carolina School of Science and Mathematics in Durham. She later earned her master’s degree in electrical engineering at N.C. State in 2002. Selected as a NASA astronaut in 2013, Koch also participated in the first all-female spacewalk during a mission aboard the International Space Station in 2019. She will serve as a mission specialist on Artemis II. More than focusing on individual milestones, Koch said the mission represents broader progress. “It’s about celebrating the fact that we’ve arrived at this place in history,” she said in a 2026 interview with The Associated Press, referring to women having the opportunity to fly to the moon. Before joining NASA, Koch spent a year working at a research station in Antarctica, an experience she said helped prepare her — and her loved ones — for long-duration missions. “So far, I haven’t gotten too many nerves from folks,” she said. “Maybe my dog, but I’ve reassured her that it’s only 10 days.” Koch has also emphasized the team effort behind space exploration. “These records and milestones aren’t about any one person,” she said during a 2023 discussion with then-N.C. State Chancellor Randy Woodson. “They’re about the fact that we collectively realize that when we do this, we have to go for all and by all.” The 47-year-old electrical engineer added that she hopes future astronauts will continue to surpass these milestones. “I can’t wait for these milestones to become normal, for the records to be broken,” Koch said. “It’s exciting to see us continue to push those boundaries.” Artemis II mission specialist Christina Koch stands in front of the crew transport vehicle during a countdown demonstration test, ...Artemis II mission specialist Christina Koch stands in front of the crew transport vehicle during a countdown demonstration test, Saturday, Dec. 20, 2025, in Cape Canaveral, Fla. (AP Photo/Phelan M. Ebenhack)Artemis II mission specialist Christina Koch stands in front of the crew transport vehicle during a countdown demonstration test, Saturday, Dec. 20, 2025, in Cape Canaveral, Fla. (AP Photo/Phelan M. Ebenhack) Artemis II will not land on the moon or enter lunar orbit, but the spacecraft will travel thousands of miles beyond it — farther than any humans have gone before — offering unprecedented views of the moon’s far side. Neither Koch nor her crewmates were alive during NASA’s Apollo program, which sent 24 astronauts to the moon, including 12 who walked on its surface. “Artemis differs from [the Apollo missions] in that even though we’re going back to the moon, this time we’re going back to stay,” Koch said. “We’re going back responsibly and sustainably.” NASA cleared its Space Launch System rocket for flight in early March and had a six-day launch window beginning Wednesday. The 32-story rocket roared to life at the Kennedy Space Center, where tens of thousands gathered to witness the launch. Crowds packed nearby roads and beaches, evoking memories of the Apollo program in the 1960s and ’70s. “On this historic mission, you take with you the heart of this Artemis team, the daring spirit of the American people and our partners across the globe, and the hopes and dreams of a new generation,” launch director Charlie Blackwell-Thompson told the crew moments before liftoff. “Good luck, Godspeed Artemis II. Let’s go.” NASA’s Artemis II moon rocket lifts off from the Kennedy Space Center’s Launch Pad 39-B Wednesday, April 1, 2026, in Cape ...NASA’s Artemis II moon rocket lifts off from the Kennedy Space Center’s Launch Pad 39-B Wednesday, April 1, 2026, in Cape Canaveral, Fla. (AP Photo/Chris O’Meara)NASA’s Artemis II moon rocket lifts off from the Kennedy Space Center’s Launch Pad 39-B Wednesday, April 1, 2026, in Cape Canaveral, Fla. (AP Photo/Chris O’Meara) Artemis II lifted off from the same launch site that once sent Apollo astronauts to the moon. Some of the few remaining Apollo-era astronauts looked on as this new generation began its journey, with a nearly full moon hanging in the distance roughly 248,000 miles away. About five minutes into flight, commander Reid Wiseman spotted the crew’s destination. “We have a beautiful moonrise — we’re headed right at it,” Wiseman said from the capsule. “NASA is back in the business of sending astronauts to the moon,” Jared Isaacman told reporters after liftoff, calling the decades-long gap a “brief intermission.” This launch marks NASA’s most significant step yet toward establishing a sustained human presence on the moon. The Artemis program is expected to culminate in a lunar landing, currently targeted for 2028. — The Associated Press contributed to this report
